## Agenda

1. Opening Exercise: Interpreting Data
2. Bias vs. Noise
3. Standard Errors
4. P-Values

## An Interpretation

Imagine an experiment with two treatments, Treatment 1 and Treatment 2. The outcome is a binary measure of vote choice: whether one votes for Party A. Participants are randomly assigned to T1, T2, or the control (no treatment).

40% of the control group votes for Party A, 45% of those in T1 vote for Party A, and 50% of those in T2 vote for Party A.

\small
**My interpretation:** Participants under Treatment 1 were 5-percentage points more likely to vote for Party A than those in the control. Participants under Treatment 2 were 10-percentage points more likely to vote for Party A than the control. These results prove that both treatments would increase vote choice for Party A among the general population. Treatment 2 would also be the more effective treatment at increasing Party A's vote choice if we ran this study again.

\normalsize
**What's wrong with this interpretation? What's correct about it?**

::: notes
It depends! My point is that we know, for this sample, the effect was that large. But we need a way of showing that this effect is particularly large.
:::

## What Do We Know?

\small

- In this sample, Treatment 1 increased vote for Party A by 5-percentage points relative to the control
- In this sample, Treatment 2 increased vote for Party A by 10-percentage points relative to the control
- In this sample, Treatment 2 increased vote for Party A by 5-percentage points more than Treatment 1 did relative to the control
- In short, we know we have an average treatment effect, but we don't know the true treatment effect
    - We never see everyone's outcomes on both treatments and control! Just on one assignment!
    - So we sampled participants and then randomly assigned treatment/control within our sample
    - What if we had sampled different participants? What if we had assigned treatment differently?
- We need a way to measure how confident we are that the findings in this study represent a true average treatment effect.
    - We can never prove that they do, but we can increase our confidence that what we found is not a coincidence.

## Bias

- Bias is a systematic deviation from the truth
- You can think of bias as a consistent inaccuracy
- You've already seen bias!
- Similar to bias in a colloquial sense:
    - If the judicial system is racially biased, it will be consistently discriminatory
    - If I have a biased point of view, I will automatically come to the same conclusion regardless of the evidence you present to me
    - If we have a biased way of researching our topic of interest, we will end up at the same (wrong) conclusion

##


## Noise

- Noise is simply the random difference between samples
- Noise is inevitable when sampling -- we don't have the true population
- This was our concern with the opening example!

## The 1936 Election: Landon vs Roosevelt

- Literary Digest did one of the largest political polls (at the time) asking 2.4 million people who would win the 1936 presidential election
    - Their prediction: \hlred{Landon = 57\%} vs \hlblue{Roosevelt = 43\%}
- Their method: Ask 10 million people on telephone lists, magazine subscription lists, club and association rosters, to fill out a mock ballot

\vspace{0.5em}
\centering
In reality: \hlred{Landon = 38\%} vs \hlblue{Roosevelt = 62\%}

\vspace{0.5em}
```{r, out.height="0.28\\textheight", fig.show="hold", fig.align="center"}
knitr::include_graphics(c("images/landon.jpg", "images/roosevelt.jpg"))
```

::: notes
Bias insofar as who was sampled; noise insofar as any poll has noise.
:::

## 1. Standard Deviation

A measure of "spread" -- summary of how much a set of values are away from the mean


The formula is:
$$
\text{SD} = \sqrt{ \frac{\sum (x - \bar{x})^2}{n-1}}
$$
## Standard Deviation

```{r, out.height="0.8\\textheight", fig.align="center"}
knitr::include_graphics("images/sd_curves.png")
```

## 2. Standard Error

- If we took a bunch of samples and measured a value for each, the standard error is the standard deviation of those values.
- In other words, standard error is a measure of how much we'd expect our findings to vary if we could replicate our study thousands of times
- Therefore, the standard error helps us measure how much we'd expect the estimate from the experiment to differ from the truth (the real effect) by chance
- It is a measure of noise, not bias

## Standard Error and its relationship to other sample statistics

$$s_{\bar{x}} = \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}$$

- $n$ = Sample size (i.e., number of observations)
- $s$ = Sample standard deviation
- $s_{\bar{x}}$ = Estimated standard error of the mean ($s/\sqrt{n}$)

::: notes
Ask them what they think happens to the SE as the s or n increases.
:::

## Standard Error and its relationship to other sample statistics

- It can only be positive
- As the standard deviation increases, the SE increases
    - Why?
- As the sample size increases, the SE decreases
    - Why?

## 3. t-statistic

$$t = \frac{\text{Estimate}}{\text{Standard Error}}$$

- **t-statistic:** to measure how likely that an estimate of the size we saw would arise by chance, even if the treatment had no effect.
- **Estimate:** our best guess of what the true ATE is.
- If $t > 1.96$ or $t < -1.96$, the observed result is **statistically significant** (more in next weeks).

```{r, out.width="\\textwidth", fig.align="center"}
knitr::include_graphics("images/t_example_output.png")
```

## Interpreting T-Statistics

```{r, out.width="\\textwidth", fig.align="center"}
knitr::include_graphics("images/regression_output.png")
```

\small
0.01857536 / 0.01099631 = 1.689236

**A small estimate relative to a large standard error will result in a small t-statistic (and less confidence in the estimate being different from zero).**

## Hypothesis Testing

\small

- In science we test hypotheses
    - Ex: Autocracies are more likely than democracies to go to war
- The **null hypothesis** is our default: what the world would look like if we did not observe the effect we are interested in finding
    - Ex: Autocracies and democracies are equally likely to go to war
- The **alternative hypothesis** reflects what we would observe if there was, actually, a true effect in the world
    - Ex: Autocracies and democracies are not equally likely to go to war
- We never prove one hypothesis or the other
    - Because of noise (i.e. sampling), we can never be sure we're observing the truth
    - But we can measure how likely we'd be to observe the effect we see by chance

## P-Values

\small

- What's the probability that we would observe the effect we see by chance?
    - A p-value of 0.13 means that there is a 13% probability that we would observe the effect we see even if the null hypothesis was true
- We want to maximize our confidence that we are NOT observing the effect by chance
    - A p-value of greater than (or equal to) 0.05 is considered statistically insignificant
    - A p-value of less than 0.05 is statistically significant
        - We are less than 5% likely to observe this effect by chance!
        - OR: We are more than 95% likely to not be observing this effect by chance!
- This gives us evidence in support of the alternative hypothesis but does not prove it

## Interpreting P-Values

```{r, out.width="\\textwidth", fig.align="center"}
knitr::include_graphics("images/regression_output.png")
```

- The treatment increases the outcome by about 1.9 percentage-points relative to the control.
- However, we would expect this result (or something smaller) to occur roughly 9% of the time if this effect was driven entirely by chance.

## Recap

\small

- We want to show that our findings are not due to chance
    - This arises from concerns about noise
    - Different sampling methods and differences in randomization could lead to slightly different results
- Standard errors show how much our results would vary across multiple versions of the same study
    - How much "error" (difference) in our outcome should we expect across samples?
- We test hypotheses to provide support for one vs. another
    - We never provide definitive proof for any hypothesis!
    - But p-values show us how probable our results would be if they arose due to chance and not due to a treatment effect
